newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Hunting consumer spending clues.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Hunting consumer spending clues.

text.p: U.S. credit markets will scrutinize fresh weekly retail store sales data on Tuesday in search of clues that could indicate how consumers are behaving during the holiday shopping season, analysts said.
"The key numbers tomorrow are going to be the retail indicators," said Patrick Dimick, Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities.
Consumers are seen by many as the wild card in the fourth quarter. If consumption rises, economic growth is likely to pick up. If it doesn't, the economy is seen slowing further.

On Tuesday, the Bank of Tokyo Mitsubishi/Schroder will release their chain store sales index for the week ended November 30. The indicator, which will be issued at 0900 EST/1400 GMT, dropped 0.5 last week.
At 1455 EST/1955, the Lynch, Jones & Ryan Inc Redbook retail sales index for the November 30 week will be released. The index was down 1.0 percent in the previous week.

Market players grew wary after news reports Monday said retailers reported stronger sales over Thanksgiving than had been expected. The reports also said shoppers appeared to be willing to spend despite lofty debt levels.
"I'm very interested to see if the Mitsubishi and the Redbook picked up the same sort of late November retail strength," Dimick said.
The rationale behind the market's concerns is simple: Stronger year-end spending could trim retailers' inventories, jump-start a slowing manufacturing sector and boost the service sector.
The possible resulting warm-up of the economy could then eventually prompt the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, which is seen as bad for bonds.
But traders said the consensus on Wall Street still appears to be that the Fed will keep monetary policy on hold for the rest of the year.
"I think that all we have so far are some jitters. We still need more data. No one is changing their minds," said a trader at U.S. investment bank.

On Tuesday, the market will also take in the new home sales numbers for October. The indicator, which will be released at 1000 EST/1500 GMT, is expected to drop to 772,000 units from 816,000 in the previous month.

Despite the mild consolidation selling seen on Monday, analysts said the market's underlying trend remains bullish, bolstered largely by a steady flow of foreign capital into U.S. Treasuries, analysts said.
"A lot of (the rally) has been fueled by what's happening abroad. Lower interest rates abroad make the U.S. look more attractive," said James Glassman, senior economist at chase Securities Inc.
Glassman also mentioned a firm dollar in the foreign currency markets as a positive factor for the domestic bond market.
"The dollar is also firmer...So you have a feeling that it's the capital flows that are driving the U.S. (bond) market right now," he said.

On Monday, the 6-1/2-percent benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was quoted down 1/32 at 101-27/32 in late trading after having rallied almost a full point by the close on Friday. Its yield was at 6.36 percent.
The Federal Reserve, facing a strong reserve need in the banking system, added reserves on Monday through overnight and three-day system repurchase agreements.
At the time of the intervention, the federal funds changed hands at 5-3/4 percent, well above the central bank's 5-1/4 percent target.
Analysts said the Fed is now expected to add permanent reserves to the system through a coupon pass operation.
"The move is expected to take place any day now and it might as well be tomorrow (Tuesday)," the trader said.
